title: The Contrast Check: Keep Your Style, Make the Outfit Easier to Read
subtitle: A wearer-led way to find clothing combinations that are easier for you to distinguish—without handing over the decisions or narrowing your palette.
imageAlt: An older family member points to a preferred outfit pairing while a couple holds up two clothing options for comparison.
imageConcept: An adult couple and an older family member gather around a bed or clothing rail with a few favorite garments laid out in pairs. The older family member is clearly directing the comparison, choosing or rejecting combinations, while the couple offers options rather than dressing them. Natural, comfortable light; no clinical equipment or staged makeover cues.
body: Getting dressed is personal, but deciding whether two pieces work together can take extra effort when low vision makes colors or shapes harder to distinguish. That challenge does not mean someone needs a new wardrobe, a strict color code or another person to choose for them. A short contrast check can help identify combinations that are easier for the wearer to see, while keeping their taste in charge. The aim is not to discover a universally “right” palette. It is to learn what works for one person, in their clothes, under the conditions where they get dressed.
Contrast is a tool, not a style rule

Contrast describes how clearly one thing stands apart from another. In clothing, that might mean a shirt that is easy to distinguish from trousers, or a jacket whose outline reads clearly against a top. Two pieces can be different colors yet feel similar in tone; black and navy, for example, are used as an illustration of colors that can be difficult to tell apart in guidance on accessible communication [3]. That example is a prompt to test a particular pairing, not a ban on wearing those colors together. The wearer’s vision, preferences and setting matter more than a general rule.

Choose a few pieces the wearer already enjoys wearing: perhaps two tops and two bottoms, or a favorite jacket and several shirts. A small selection keeps the exercise manageable and makes it easier to compare options without turning a closet into a sorting project. Lay garments flat or hang them side by side, whichever lets the wearer examine them most comfortably. Use the lighting they prefer for getting dressed. The American Academy of Ophthalmology includes increasing contrast, reducing glare and improving lighting among low-vision techniques [1]. In practice, that means checking whether the comparison is comfortable and clear—not simply making the room as bright as possible. If light reflects off a surface or feels unpleasant, adjust the setup.
Let the wearer set the pace

Before starting, agree on the companion’s role. A useful opening is: “Would you like me to hold up a few options, describe what I see, or just listen while you compare?” The wearer can choose one garment to compare with another, ask for a description or stop at any point. A companion might say, “This shirt looks much darker than these trousers to me,” then pause for the wearer’s response. Avoid replacing that observation with a verdict such as “That doesn’t match.” The person wearing the outfit decides whether the combination feels right, whether it is easy enough to identify and whether they want help at all.
Compare one thing at a time

Start with two garments and ask a practical question: Can the wearer distinguish them as separate pieces in this light? Try another pairing, then switch one item and compare again. Keep the conditions as steady as possible—same room, same lighting, same viewing distance—so that the comparison is about the clothes rather than a sudden change in setup. The AAO recommends contrasting colors to make household features easier to distinguish [2]. That household advice does not prescribe clothing choices, but it supports the broader idea of testing whether contrast helps in a specific visual task. Here, the test is personal: one person may find a particular pairing clear; another may not.

When a pairing feels easier to distinguish, note it in a way the wearer likes. That might be a short list, a phone note, or a garment tag the wearer can identify. Use the result to put together two or three ready-to-wear combinations from existing favorites. Keep the descriptions concrete: “striped top with charcoal trousers” is more useful than “the good outfit,” especially if someone else may help locate the pieces later. If several combinations work, there is no need to reduce the wardrobe to one dependable formula. The point is to make choices easier to revisit, not to turn personal style into a uniform.
Add a non-color cue only if it helps

Color does not have to carry all the information. If two items remain hard to tell apart, the wearer might choose another cue that fits their habits: a different texture, a distinctive button, or a discreet label. A tactile marker can help identify a garment without relying on color alone; lighting and contrast guidance for low vision also discusses tactile labels as an optional source of information [1]. Keep any marker comfortable, secure and easy for the wearer to interpret. Ask before adding anything, and let the wearer decide where it belongs. There is no need to label every item if a few favorite combinations are already straightforward.
Keep the check small and revisable

A hands-on comparison at home can be simpler: choose a few garments, test them in the wearer’s preferred lighting, and keep only the information they find useful. Try this once with a favorite outfit and one alternative. Let the wearer name what is easiest to distinguish, what they enjoy wearing and what they would change. A useful result might be a single reliable pairing, a clearer description, or the decision that the original outfit is already right. The clothes remain theirs, and the method can change whenever their preferences do.
